title: Secure submission management starts with counting the copies
summary: Secure submission management starts with counting how many copies of a broker submission your process makes. Where copies come from and how to cut them.
body_markdown:
Secure submission management means a broker submission lives in as few places as possible between arrival and quote, and every copy that does exist sits under a control your security team can name and test. Here is a quick way to see where you stand. Take one renewal from last week and write down every place its loss runs live today. You will get the shared inbox, then the forward to the underwriter and another to the assistant. Someone saved the PDF to a desktop to rekey the schedule. The clearance spreadsheet has the FEIN in column D. If part of intake is outsourced, add a second company's mailbox and file share. That package might hold driver license numbers, payroll by class code and audited financials, sometimes inside a 500-page PDF that is really nine documents stapled together. A vendor questionnaire asks how well one vendor guards its copy. Counting copies tells you how many there are to guard, and few teams have ever written that number down.


## What does secure submission management mean for a carrier or MGA?


Secure submission management is the practice of keeping submission data inside a small, known set of systems, with access by role, a log of who touched what and a clear rule for when working copies are deleted. The regulatory reasons to care keep adding up for commercial, specialty and E&S carriers and MGAs, and they reach well beyond the policy admin system. According to the[New York Department of Financial Services](https://www.dfs.ny.gov/industry_guidance/cybersecurity) , its cybersecurity regulation, 23 NYCRR Part 500, has required covered entities to run risk-informed cybersecurity policies and programs since March 1, 2017. The[NAIC Insurance Data Security Model Law (#668)](https://content.naic.org/insurance-topics/cybersecurity) asks licensees to develop, implement and maintain an information security program, investigate cybersecurity events and notify the state insurance commissioner, and the NAIC's own topic page, last updated in May 2024, counts 21 states that have adopted it. Where AI is part of the workflow, the[NAIC model bulletin on the use of AI by insurers](https://content.naic.org/insurance-topics/artificial-intelligence) , adopted in December 2023, states that decisions made or supported by AI must comply with all applicable insurance laws and regulations, which brings the data feeding those decisions into scope as well.


## Where do the copies of a broker submission come from?


Most copies of a submission are made for good operational reasons by people trying to move a file faster, which is why they rarely show up on a data map until someone traces a real file end to end. When we walk a single commercial submission through a manual or partly outsourced intake process, the copies usually come from four places:


- The shared submissions mailbox, plus every forward to an underwriter, an assistant or an outside team, each of which leaves the full attachment set in another inbox.
- Attachments saved to shared drives, desktops or download folders so someone can rekey the ACORD forms, schedules and loss runs into another system.
- Clearance and status trackers, often spreadsheets, that hold the insured name, FEIN, address, broker and premium indication for every file in the pipeline.
- An outsourced or offshore processing team working in its own email, ticketing and file storage, which puts a second organization's systems inside your data flow.


The copies in your policy admin system and rater belong there, since they are the system of record that your security program already covers. The working copies are the ones to count, and the table below is the format we suggest for the count, with one row per copy and an honest answer in every cell.


Working copy Why it gets made Who can usually see it Question for your security team


Forwarded submission emails Routing a file to the right underwriter or team Everyone on the thread, plus anyone with access to those inboxes How long do forwarded attachments stay in personal mailboxes?


Saved attachments on drives or desktops Rekeying forms and schedules into another system Whoever has access to that folder or laptop Is there a deletion rule once the data is keyed?


Clearance and status spreadsheets Tracking files that sit outside the core system Often the whole underwriting team, sometimes brokers' contacts too Does the tracker hold FEINs or financial data it does not need?


Outsourced team systems Extraction and data entry handled by a third party The provider's staff, tools and subcontractors Is the provider in your third-party risk program, with evidence on file?


## Why does outsourced submission processing add copies?


Outsourced submission processing adds copies by design, since the work moves to a second organization that needs its own mailboxes, file shares and production tools to do it, and each of those systems becomes part of the data flow your information security program has to cover. We have no quarrel with the people doing that work, who are often careful and well trained, and the issue we see is structural, in that a person-based process needs the document to travel to the person. An AI-native service changes the direction of travel, because the extraction, the clearance checks and the human review all happen inside one system where access is set by role and every action lands in the same activity log. In practice that means a reviewer who corrects a field does it on the record that already exists, so the review step adds a line to the audit trail and no new copy of the submission.

The person checking a field works on the record that already sits in the AI Underwriting OS, under the same access rules and log as the extraction. Straight-through mode skips human review for speed-first, simpler risks and returns results instantly. ## Which controls should cover the copies you keep?


Some working copies will always exist, so the next job is to put each remaining one under a control your security team can test and an examiner can follow without a guided tour. One distinction helps early on: AI in an underwriting workflow reads documents and applies your rules, and it does not manage your infrastructure, network security or access control, so those stay with your team and your vendors' security programs. Here is what we ask about first:


- Single sign-on with access by role, line and program, so an assistant, an underwriter and an outside reviewer each see only what their job needs.
- Identity for the software itself, with short-lived credentials for automated work, since an AI agent that reads a mailbox is a user too and should be logged like one.
- An activity log with data lineage that records the source document, the extracted value and every human change, with who made it and when.
- A written retention and deletion rule for working copies, including attachments saved during rekeying and files sent to any third party.
- Current SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001 evidence from every provider that touches submission data, read by your own team, plus plain data-use terms that say whether your submissions train models serving other customers.


For a deeper version of the vendor questions, our guide on[what carriers must verify before trusting an AI vendor](https://www.pibit.ai/blog/data-security-underwriting-automation-what-carriers-must-verify) covers certifications, residency and model isolation, and our piece on[PII redaction in commercial P&C submission intake](https://www.pibit.ai/blog/pii-redaction-commercial-pc-submission-intake-regulatory-layer) goes into how personal data is handled field by field.


## How can an underwriting operations lead cut the copy count in 30 days?


A 30-day copy count is a practical project that an underwriting operations lead can run with one person from IT security, and it usually produces a shorter list of fixes than a full security assessment would. The steps we suggest are these:


1. **Trace three real submissions.** Pick one small, one mid-sized and one complex file, and follow each from the broker's email to the issued quote, writing down every inbox, folder, spreadsheet and outside system it touched.
2. **Label every copy.** Mark each one as system of record or working copy, and note who can see it and how long it lives.
3. **Close the easy gaps first.** Turn off automatic forwarding from the submissions mailbox to personal inboxes, and set a deletion rule for attachments saved during rekeying.
4. **Move clearance tracking into the intake system.** Retire the spreadsheet that holds FEINs and premium indications once the intake record can show status by itself.
5. **Ask each third party where its copies live.** Request a written answer from any outsourcing provider or software vendor on storage, access, retention and deletion, and file it with their security evidence.
6. **Start with one stage.** Put intake and clearance under one controlled system first, measure the new copy count, and only then move on to extraction and triage.


Teams that already follow[submission intake best practices](https://www.pibit.ai/blog/submission-intake-best-practices-commercial-pc) will find that most of the work in steps three and four is about removing workarounds that grew up around a slow intake process, which is why speed and security tend to improve together once intake itself is fixed.
